evidence.paraphrase: A shipwrecked emigrant is cast onto an English shore that is entirely foreign to him, an undiscovered country.
evidence.quote:
he was a castaway. A poor emigrant from Central Europe bound to
America and washed ashore here in a storm. And for him, who knew nothing
of the earth, England was an undiscovered country.

evidence.paraphrase: The castaway believed he was no longer alive in the ordinary world after being washed ashore.
evidence.quote:
he told me himself that
he put his trust in God, believing he was no longer in this world. And
truly--he would add--how was he to know?

evidence.paraphrase: The mountaineer perceives ordinary travelers as vast multitudes dressed like the rich, contrasting his rural frame of reference with modern industrial society.
evidence.quote:
He gave me to understand
that he had on his passage beheld uncounted multitudes of people--whole
nations--all dressed in such clothes as the rich wear.

evidence.paraphrase: A railway station is described through the uncomprehending eyes of the mountaineer, who lacks words for trains and glass roofs.
evidence.quote:
There was a roof over him, which
seemed made of glass, and was so high that the tallest mountain-pine
he had ever seen would have had room to grow under it. Steam-machines
rolled in at one end and out at the other.

evidence.paraphrase: The emigrant recruiters exploit the peasants' ignorance, who imagine a telegraph as a device to speak to an 'Emperor of America.'
evidence.quote:
in the next room,
so that the common people shouldn t hear, they kept a cunning telegraph
machine, through which they could talk to the Emperor of America.

evidence.paraphrase: The emigrant ship carrying the castaway sank in Eastbay, a notorious disaster.
evidence.quote:
the vessel sunk the night before in Eastbay was the Hamburg emigrant-ship
_Herzogin Sophia-Dorothea_, of appalling memory.

evidence.paraphrase: The ship capsized and sank completely, leaving no trace above water, with drowned bodies washing ashore.
evidence.quote:
The Hamburg ship, filling all at once, capsized as she sank, and at daylight
there was not even the end of a spar to be seen above water.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains that fraudulent emigration agencies exploited poor peasants to seize their homesteads.
evidence.quote:
A few months later we could read in the papers the accounts of the
bogus  Emigration Agencies  among the Sclavonian peasantry in the more
remote provinces of Austria.

evidence.paraphrase: Kennedy is characterized as possessing a scientific, investigative mind that seeks truth in every mystery.
evidence.quote:
His intelligence
is of a scientific order, of an investigating habit, and of that
unappeasable curiosity which believes that there is a particle of a
general truth in every mystery.

evidence.paraphrase: Kennedy systematically tests hypotheses about the stranger's origin by trying different languages on him.
evidence.quote:
It occurred to
me he might be a Basque. It didn t necessarily follow that he should
understand Spanish; but I tried him with the few words I know, and also
with some French.

evidence.paraphrase: Smith reacts with dread and takes the stranger for an escaped lunatic upon their inexplicable encounter.
evidence.quote:
Smith, alone amongst his stacks with this apparition, in
the stormy twilight ringing with the infuriated barking of the dog, felt
the dread of an inexplicable strangeness.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator likens the castaway's alienation among the villagers to a man transplanted to another planet.
evidence.quote:
this castaway, that, like a man transplanted into
another planet, was separated by an immense space from his past and
by an immense ignorance from his future.

evidence.paraphrase: The castaway experienced overwhelming loneliness, perceiving the villagers as faces of dead people from another world.
evidence.quote:
It was as if these had been the
faces of people from the other world--dead people--he used to tell me
years afterwards. Upon my word, I wonder he did not go mad.

evidence.paraphrase: Kennedy offers a medical explanation for the stranger's illness, attributing it to lung trouble and failure to acclimatise.
evidence.quote:
At all events, the next time I saw
him he was ill--lung trouble. He was tough, but I daresay he was not
acclimatised as well as I had supposed.

evidence.paraphrase: Amy is overcome by an unreasonable terror of the husband she cannot understand as he lies feverish.
evidence.quote:
the terror, the unreasonable terror, of that man she
could not understand creeping over her.

evidence.paraphrase: The mutual incomprehension drives Amy to flee in fear from her dying husband, leaving him helpless.
evidence.quote:
She jumped to her feet, snatched up the child, and stood still. He
spoke to her, and his passionate remonstrances only increased her
fear of that strange man.

evidence.paraphrase: The dying castaway, abandoned and thirsty, cries out demanding to know why, addressing his Maker.
evidence.quote:
Why?  he cried in the penetrating and indignant
voice of a man calling to a responsible Maker.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator frames the castaway's death as the ultimate consequence of his utter loneliness and estrangement.
evidence.quote:
the father, cast out mysteriously by
the sea to perish in the supreme disaster of loneliness and despair.
